newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Frustrated Ansett eyes Macau for extra flights.
newsitem.headline: Frustrated Ansett eyes Macau for extra flights.

text.p: HONG KONG, Feb 28 - (Reuter) Ansett Australia, frustrated at being denied daily flights to Hong Kong, is doing a feasibility study into starting direct flights to nearby Macau, said the airline's Hong Kong general manager Bob Evans.

The Australian carrier, which operates five Boeing 747-300 flights a week between Hong Kong and Sydney, has repeatedly failed to win regulatory approval to begin a daily service. In an interview Evans told Reuters the Macau option could complement the carrier's Hong Kong service but not replace it.

"I would emphasise we are not trying to use Macau as a bargaining position against Hong Kong but at the moment we are hamstrung by a government to government matter from competing effectively on an important route," Evans said.

A daily Sydney-Hong Kong service is Ansett's "minimum position" before applying for more links to other Australinn gateways such as Melbourne. Ansett has recently been successful in increasing capacity to Osaka in Japan and starts to Shanghai on June 8.
"Daily flights to Hong Kong are essential for a credible service. Business travellers who need flexible travel plans especially need to know there are daily flights," he added.
Evans said cargo traffic between Hong Kong and Sydney was "very very strong" with inter-line traffic from the UK playing an important part.

"We are not only handling ex China traffic but we have interline agreements, for instance with European carriers such as Virgin Atlantic, and are being very successful despite not being able to offer a daily service from Hong Kong", Evans said.
Industry observers said a new round of bilateral talks between Hong Kong and Australia are due to be held in April when Ansett will again press for increased frequency.

Alternatively, Macau's new 24 hour airport, free from slot restrictions which affect Kai Tak users, is very keen to attract more international airlines and an Australian link would be very welcome, industry observers said. To compensate for the hour long sea transfer, cheaper landing fees in the Portuguese enclave could also mean lower fares, the observers added.
